evidence_quote: The 253 sixth grade participants were recruited for the after-school program from four intermediate schools in a school district in west Tennessee.

evidence_quote: we restricted the eligible population to students who scored in the bottom 20 percent (statewide) or significantly below grade level on the state standardized reading test.
resolved_title: Putting Computerized Instruction to the Test: A Randomized Evaluation of a Scientifically Based Reading Program (Rouse and Krueger, 2004)
notes: Fast ForWord evaluation in four urban schools. evidence_quote: The trial was to involve, ideally, two classes of Y5 pupils per school, and the same pupils when they progress into Y6. The target recruitment was for two-form entry schools wherever possible.
resolved_title: ScratchMaths: Evaluation report and executive summary (Boylan et al., 2018, EEF)
notes: Whole Year 5 cohort in 110 randomised schools; the only school criteria were form entry, internet connectivity, and enough computers. Kraft n 5818 is the full KS2 maths sample and n 1632 is the everFSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so one of the two Kraft effects is a subgroup. UK Year 5 is US grade 4.

evidence_quote: Schools were required to have sufficient numbers of EAL pupils (absolute minimum of ten in Y5 for 2016/2017, lowered to eight following slow uptake during the early recruitment period), identified using a binary EAL/not EAL measure to enable subgroup analysis.
resolved_title: Integrating English: Evaluation Report (Culliney, Moore, Coldwell, and Demack, 2019, EEF)
notes: All Year 5 pupils in 91 randomised two-form-entry primary schools took part. The only school rule was a minimum of eight to ten EAL pupils, stated as a requirement for subgroup analysis rather than selection on need, so coded universal with medium confidence; a reviewer could read it as targeted_other at school level. Kraft n 3607 is the full sample and n 1291 is likely the FSM or EAL subgroup, so one of the three effects is a subgroup.

evidence_quote: Once the school confirmed the uniformed group to be offered, the lead contact person in the school ran a recruitment drive to attract pupils. The target pupils were those in Year 9 (aged 13/14). Pupils were recruited at the end of Year 8.
resolved_title: Youth Social Action Trials: Youth United. Evaluation report and executive summary (Gorard, See, Siddiqui, Smith, and White, 2016, EEF)

evidence_quote: The programme was targeted at pupils aged nine to 11 (Years 5 and 6) who were eligible for FSM, had low literacy scores, English as an additional language, or a special educational need.
resolved_title: Future Foundations: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary (Gorard, Siddiqui, and See, 2014, EEF)
notes: Summer school with individual randomisation. Eligibility was disjunctive (FSM, low literacy, EAL, or SEN); the executive summary (PDF p. 4) phrases it as FSM-eligible pupils and pupils who had not achieved Level 4 in English or maths at KS2. Coded targeted_low under tie-breaker 1 because a performance criterion was part of the rule, but a reviewer could prefer targeted_other since not every pupil was selected on achievement. Participation voluntary (summer holiday). Kraft n 306-310 is the overall achieved sample; FSM-only and Year 5 results are also reported, hence mixed_samples 1 as a caution.

evidence_quote: All schools have, or recently had, at least 25% of their pupils known to be eligible for free school meals (FSM). At least 10 of the schools had fewer than 60% of pupils achieving Level 4+ in English and maths, and with pupils making below-average progress in English and maths, in 2012 (or 2011). These were therefore disadvantaged schools.
resolved_title: Philosophy for Children: Evaluation report and Executive summary (Gorard, Siddiqui, and See, 2015, EEF)
notes: 48 primary schools recruited on an FSM threshold (at least 25 percent) and randomised; all Year 4 and Year 5 pupils in the schools took part, so the rule is at school level and on poverty. The low-attainment description applies to only some schools and is descriptive, not a criterion. Kraft five effects with n 498-1529 span the full sample and the pre-specified FSM-only analyses (Tables 8-10), so some effects are a subgroup.

evidence_quote: Pupils were eligible as long as they were in the bottom 15-20% of mathematics achievement based on attainment at KS1, as well as the professional judgement of teachers based on their more recent performance.
resolved_title: Catch Up Numeracy: Evaluation report and executive summary (Hodgen, Adkins, Ainsworth, and Evans, 2019, EEF)
notes: Schools recruited by the developer had to provide at least six eligible Year 4 and six eligible Year 5 pupils (or four in each of Years 3 to 5); that is a capacity requirement, not school selection on need, so level is student. Kraft n 1481 matches the primary model and n 551 the everFSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so one of the two effects is a subgroup. Report notes schools interpreted the eligibility criterion broadly.

evidence_quote: The target cohort within the schools were pupils in Year 4 (Y4) and Year 5 (Y5) in the first year of the trial (2016/2017). After accounting for parental/carer opt-outs (n = 117; 0.91%), this sample consisted of n = 6,586 and n = 6,338 pupils in the Y4 and Y5 cohorts, respectively.
resolved_title: Achievement for All Evaluation Report (Humphrey, Squires, Choudry, Byrne, Demkowicz, Troncoso, and Wo, 2020, EEF)
notes: Whole-school programme; 134 schools recruited by the developer (only rule: not previously involved with AfA) and randomised; all Y5 pupils analysed. Schools nominated a 20 percent AfA target group of vulnerable pupils, but the headline analysis is the whole cohort. Kraft n 5813 is the complete-case whole-cohort KS2 reading sample and n 1231 the FSM subgroup (ES -0.157 in the FSM table), so one of the two effects is a subgroup. Hand-supplied PDF.

evidence_quote: The parents of all pupils in Years 3 to 6 of the 16 recruited schools were invited to take part in the intervention. Of those, 2,690 pupils in 2,306 distinct families did not opt out.
resolved_title: Parent Academy: Evaluation report and executive summary (Husain, Jabin, Haywood, Kasim, and Paylor, 2016, EEF)
notes: Pupil-level randomisation among all Years 3 to 6 pupils whose parents did not opt out, in 16 schools recruited on a convenience basis in two local authorities; intention to treat, so opt_in 0 even though parents chose whether to attend the academy. Kraft n 1465-1578 does not match the report analysed samples of 1,895 (reading) and 1,923 (maths); the four Kraft effects may include the FSM-only analysis or the adjusted models. No achievement rule.

evidence_quote: Eligible schools were those having at least two Year 5 classes and a high proportion (over 20%) of children eligible for free school meals (FSM pupils).
resolved_title: Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary (Jay et al., 2017, EEF)
notes: 78 schools in Leeds, Bradford, and Birmingham recruited on an FSM threshold and randomised; all Year 5 pupils in the schools took part. Analysed sample was 1,832 intervention and 2,080 control pupils, so Kraft n 603-1239 does not match the full sample; 1,239 and 603 appear in secondary-outcome and subgroup tables, so Kraft effects appear to come from subsamples.

evidence_quote: Ten secondary schools in North East England were recruited to take part in the trial, selecting schools where the proportion of pupils eligible for free school meals (FSM) was above the national average.
resolved_title: Paired Reading: Evaluation report and Executive summary (Lloyd, Edovald, Kiss, Morris, Skipp, and Ahmed, 2015, EEF)
notes: Class-level randomisation; all Year 7 (tutee) and Year 9 (tutor) classes in the schools were eligible, with extra classes dropped only to equalise numbers. Kraft n 1300 (Year 7) and 1265 (Year 9) match the adjusted analyses. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Kennedy, Deshler, and Lloyd 2015) and was ignored. UK Years 7 and 9 are US grades 6 and 8.

evidence_quote: Schools were eligible to participate in the project if they were a mainstream state secondary school in any area of England willing to be randomised to implementing the intervention (and pay a contribution of 10,000 pounds) or to be part of a business as usual control group.
resolved_title: Project Based Learning: Evaluation report and executive summary (Menzies et al., 2016, EEF)
notes: 24 secondary schools randomised; all Year 7 pupils in participating schools were included. No need-based rule; schools self-selected and paid. Pound sign in the quote replaced with the word pounds.

evidence_quote: Within participating schools, all pupils in Years 7, 9 and 11 were eligible for inclusion.

evidence_quote: the study used three criteria to identify potential districts and schools: (1) geographical diversity, (2) high poverty rates, and (3) enough teachers volunteering for the study. resolved_title: Effectiveness of Reading and Mathematics Software Products: Findings from the First Student Cohort (Dynarski et al., 2007, NCEE 2007-4005)

Districts and schools recruited on high poverty and Title I; the report also says the team focused on districts with low student achievement but calls that a general guideline rather than a strict eligibility criterion (PDF p. 25), so coded on poverty. Teachers volunteered and were randomized within schools; all their students included. Twin of 1044 (same trial, same n and ES).

resolved_title: Children's University: Evaluation report and executive summary (Gorard, Siddiqui, See, Smith, and White, 2017, EEF)
notes: 68 schools recruited by Children's University regional offices and randomised; Years 5 and 6. Kraft n 1231 matches the volunteer KS2 maths and reading analyses and n 493 the everFSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so two of the four effects are a subgroup. No achievement rule.

evidence_quote: it was intended that around 40 per cent of schools in the study sample were to be or have been below the government performance floor target threshold at some time in the last three years ... The local authorities were asked to prioritise schools that were perceived as having weaknesses in maths teaching
resolved_title: Durham Shared Maths Project: Evaluation report and Executive summary (Lloyd, Edovald, Morris, Kiss, Skipp, and Haywood, 2015, EEF)
notes: Cluster RCT in 82 schools across four local authorities; all Year 3 and Year 5 pupils in recruited schools took part, so any selection is at school level. Recruitment aims were that about 40 percent of schools be below the floor target and that schools come from high-deprivation areas, and local authorities were asked to prioritise schools with perceived weaknesses in maths teaching; these were aims, not strict criteria, so confidence is medium and a reviewer could prefer targeted_other (deprivation) or universal. Kraft n 2786 (Year 5) and 2683 (Year 3) match the analysed samples. Hand-supplied PDF; the wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Kennedy et al. 2015).

evidence_quote: The eligibility criteria for the targeted version were children who were poor at reading comprehension but relatively good at decoding. The children in this category were selected by teachers in June 2017 using guidance and materials provided by FFT literacy
resolved_title: Reciprocal Reading: Evaluation Report (O'Hare et al., 2019, EEF)
notes: Two arms in 98 schools: a universal arm delivered to all Year 4 pupils (overall reading n 3198, ES 0.00; comprehension n 2958, ES -0.02) and a targeted arm for Years 5 and 6 in which teachers selected six poor comprehenders per class (overall n 1296, ES 0.14; comprehension n 1270, ES 0.18). Kraft's four effects and n 1270-3198 span both arms, so half of the effects come from a universal whole-cohort sample; coded targeted_low because the codebook takes the first applicable code, with mixed_samples 1 so the merge can split the arms. Schools were recruited preferentially from high-FSM areas to reach a mean of at least 29 percent everFSM, but all school types could join, so level stays student.

evidence_quote: Schools were eligible to take part in the evaluation if they: (1) were willing to be randomly assigned to the intervention or control group at the year group level; (2) were willing to engage with the programme and implement with Year 9 pupils; and (3) were willing to allow the evaluation team access to pupils for administration of tests.
resolved_title: Powerful Learning Conversations: Evaluation report and executive summary (Rienzo, Rolfe, and Wilkinson, 2016, EEF)
notes: Feasibility trial in South West England secondary schools, randomised at year-group level; all Year 9 pupils in participating year groups. No need-based rule. Kraft n 1722 matches the English main analysis (Table 6) and n 276 the low-pre-attainment English subgroup (KS2 points in the bottom third), so at least one of the three effects is a subgroup. UK Year 9 is US grade 8.

evidence_quote: Schools were asked to nominate up to 12 Year 4 and Year 5 pupils, who were underperforming or struggling in literacy. There was no threshold to describe the underperformance.
resolved_title: Catch Up Literacy: Evaluation report and executive summary (Roy, Rutt, Buchanan, Rennie, Martin, and Walker, 2019, EEF)
notes: Teacher nomination of struggling readers in Years 4 and 5; schools eligible if not already using Catch Up. Kraft n 1006 matches the primary analysis and n 494 the everFSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so one of the two effects is a subgroup. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Barnett et al., SUNY placement) and was ignored. UK Years 4 and 5 are US grades 3 and 4.

evidence_quote: it recruited schools with predominantly, but not exclusively, an above average proportion of pupils eligible for FSM. resolved_title: Stop and Think: Learning Counterintuitive Concepts. Evaluation Report (Roy, Rutt, Easton, Sims, Bradshaw, and McNamara, 2019, EEF)
notes: All Year 3 and Year 5 pupils in 89 randomised primary schools. Recruitment leaned toward above-average FSM schools but the report states all primary schools with the two year groups were eligible, so coded universal with medium confidence; a reviewer could prefer targeted_other at school level. Kraft n 2702 and ES 0.09 match the maths summary table. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Barnett et al.) and was ignored.

evidence_quote: Fifty-two schools expressed an interest in participating in the study; 24 were selected by the IEE, choosing those that had low prior attainment and high levels of socio-economic deprivation (based on the proportion of pupils receiving free school meals).
resolved_title: MathsFlip: Flipped Learning. Evaluation report and executive summary (Rudd, Villanueva Aguilera, Elliott, and Chambers, 2017, EEF)
notes: Only high-FSM primary schools in Birmingham and the Black Country could express interest, and the evaluator then picked 24 on low prior attainment and deprivation; all Year 5 pupils in the schools took part, so the rule is at school level and includes a performance criterion (tie-breaker 1). Kraft n 1129 matches the KS2 maths analysis and n 426 the FSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so one of the two effects is a subgroup.

evidence_quote: Pupil participants were those from Years 3 to 6 identified as eligible. Eligibility was assessed using a combination of teacher judgements of which pupils were deemed to be unlikely to meet the Year 2 Programme of Study and the criteria in the Ofsted framework grade indicators for pupil outcomes.
resolved_title: Maths Counts: Evaluation report and executive summary (See, Morris, Gorard, and Siddiqui, 2018, EEF)
notes: Schools recruited were those with above the national average FSM percentage (school-level rule), and within each school at least eight lowest-attaining pupils were identified and individually randomised (student-level rule), so level is both. Priority also given to Pupil Premium pupils and younger KS2 pupils. Kraft n 291 is close to the 305 pupils recruited across 35 schools. Kraft grade list 2-5,10 looks odd for a Years 3 to 6 sample.

evidence_quote: To be assigned to condition, schools had to meet the following inclusion criteria: had at least 20 Year 2 students in single form entry class and 20 Year 5 students in single form entry class; ... met criteria acceptable to the EEF, in that the majority of schools in the sample would be from a disadvantaged area
resolved_title: Talk of the Town: Evaluation report and executive summary (Thurston, 2016, EEF)
notes: 64 single-form-entry primary schools randomised; all Year 2 and Year 5 pupils. The disadvantage criterion was applied to the sample as a whole (above the national FSM mean) rather than to each school, so confidence is medium; the achieved sample was about 63 percent FSM. Kraft n 2696 matches the NGRT main analysis and n 292 is the ACE secondary outcome on the full sample (not a subgroup), so mixed_samples 0. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is Miller et al. 2016 (Texting Parents), not this study. UK Years 2 and 5 are US grades 1 and 4.

evidence_quote: All Year 5 and Year 6 pupils in the 2015/2016 academic year at participating primary schools were eligible for inclusion in the study. Pupils were identified from the school roll in the 2014/2015 academic year (when they were in Years 4 and 5).
resolved_title: Calderdale Excellence Partnership: IPEELL. Evaluation report and executive summary (Torgerson et al., 2018, EEF)
notes: Twin of 899 (same report; Kraft split the two trials). This row is Trial 1, IPEELL for one year in Year 6, n 2196 with ES 0.11 matching the summary table; Kraft's second ES of -0.30 is not in the summary table and may be a secondary outcome. Whole year groups in 84 randomised schools in Leeds and Lincolnshire. Recruitment preferentially targeted schools with high FSM and high proportions below age-expected KS2 levels, but the only exclusion was Ofsted category four, so coded universal with medium confidence; a reviewer could prefer a school-level targeted code. Identical code to 899.

evidence_quote: All Year 5 and Year 6 pupils in the 2015/2016 academic year at participating primary schools were eligible for inclusion in the study. Pupils were identified from the school roll in the 2014/2015 academic year (when they were in Years 4 and 5).
resolved_title: Calderdale Excellence Partnership: IPEELL. Evaluation report and executive summary (Torgerson et al., 2018, EEF)
notes: Twin of 896 (same report; Kraft split the two trials). This row is Trial 2, IPEELL for two years from Year 5, n 2465 with ES -0.09 and the everFSM subgroup n 811 with ES 0.14, both matching the summary table, so at least one of the four effects is a subgroup. Whole year groups in randomised schools; recruitment preferentially targeted high-FSM and low-KS2 schools but the only exclusion was Ofsted category four, so coded universal with medium confidence. Identical code to 896. Text file is byte-identical to 896's.

evidence_quote: Eligibility criteria for participation required schools to be state-funded primary schools (e.g. community, foundation or academy) who have not previously implemented FRIENDS.
evidence_location: PDF p. 17, Methods, Participant selection (printed p. 16)
resolved_title: FRIENDS for Life: Evaluation report and executive summary (Education Endowment Foundation, 2018; University of Manchester repository copy)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: first page (the Manchester Research Explorer cover sheet) names Wigelsworth, Squires, Birchinall, Kalambouka, Lendrum, Black, Troncoso, Santos, Ashworth, and Britteon (EEF 2018), matching Kraft's ten surnames; the earlier pass had coded the EEF Good Behaviour Game report by mistake. Kent state-funded primary schools that had not used FRIENDS were recruited; 122 Year 5 classes in 79 schools were randomized within school, FRIENDS was delivered universally to whole classes, and parents could opt out. Most schools were below the national FSM average; no need-based rule. Kraft's n 1,534 matches the KS2 analysis sample in the report tables, and the rows are KS2 maths and reading (ES 0.00 and -0.01).

evidence_quote: The size of the recruitment pool was determined by the capacity of the intervention team to deliver the intervention to a maximum of 20 schools. The eligibility criteria included any state secondary schools.
resolved_title: The RISE Project: Evidence-informed school improvement. Evaluation Report (Wiggins, Jerrim, Tripney, Khatwa, and Gough, 2019, EEF)
notes: 40 secondary schools in Yorkshire and the Humber recruited by convenience and randomised; whole-school intervention with GCSE English and maths outcomes for full cohorts. Kraft n 6814 (maths) and 6639 (English) match the summary table. Outcomes are GCSEs taken in Year 11 (US grade 10), so Kraft's grade 8-9 listing looks off.

evidence_quote: Forty-five schools in Greater Manchester, England, were randomly assigned to treatment and control groups. Allocation was balanced by proportions of children eligible for free school meals and speaking English as an additional language via minimization. Children (N = 4516) aged 7-9 years at baseline in the participating schools were the target cohort.
resolved_title: A cluster randomized controlled trial of the Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS) curriculum (Humphrey et al., 2016, Journal of School Psychology)
notes: Abstract only. Whole age cohort in randomised schools; no student rule stated. The resolved article reports social-emotional outcomes, whereas Kraft's eight maths and reading effects (n 281-1582) must come from the EEF PATHS evaluation report of the same Manchester trial (Humphrey, Barlow, Wigelsworth et al., 2015), which reported KS2 attainment for a subsample and FSM subgroups; n 281 is likely a subgroup, hence mixed_samples 1. Kraft lists Barlow as first author, which matches neither document's author order.

evidence_quote: This paper attempts to overcome these limitations by presenting evidence from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving more than 4,000 children in England.
resolved_title: Does Teaching Children How to Play Cognitively Demanding Games Improve Their Educational Attainment? (Jerrim, Macmillan, Micklewright, Sawtell, and Wiggins, 2018, Journal of Human Resources)
notes: Abstract only; it gives no sample description beyond the count, so no eligibility rule can be read. Kraft cites the 2016 EEF Chess in Schools evaluation report by the same authors; the resolved item is the later journal version of the same trial. Kraft n 1321 does not match the abstract's more than 4,000 children. Study 995 was resolved to this same abstract but appears to be a different trial (see its note).

evidence_quote: This paper attempts to overcome these limitations by presenting evidence from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving more than 4,000 children in England.
resolved_title: Does Teaching Children How to Play Cognitively Demanding Games Improve Their Educational Attainment? (Jerrim et al., 2018, Journal of Human Resources)
notes: Resolution looks wrong: Kraft's row (Wiggins, Sawtell, Jerrim, 2017; seven maths and reading effects; n 1671-3127; grades 4-5) does not fit the chess trial abstract that was auto-accepted (one trial, more than 4,000 children, three subjects), and the abstract itself states no eligibility rule. Coded unclear from the abstract; recommend re-resolving to the 2017 EEF report by Wiggins, Sawtell, and Jerrim before merging.

evidence_quote: A total of 24 teachers and 400 children in Grades 3, 4, and 5 were randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions: control, books only, books with oral reading scaffolding, and books with oral reading and comprehension scaffolding.
resolved_title: Scaffolding Voluntary Summer Reading for Children in Grades 3 to 5: An Experimental Study (Kim and White, 2008, Scientific Studies of Reading)
notes: Abstract only. Children in the classrooms of 24 teachers randomised across four conditions; no achievement or demographic rule stated, and the abstract does not say whether every child in those classrooms was included. Voluntary refers to the summer reading, not to enrolment in the study, so opt_in 0. Kraft n 400 matches. Confidence capped at medium by the abstract-only rule.

evidence_quote: Assessment and LEarning in Knowledge Spaces (ALEKS), a technology-based mathematics curriculum, was piloted in the 2012-2013 school year at a Minnesota rural public middle school.
resolved_title: A Mathematics Education Comparative Analysis of ALEKS Technology and Direct Classroom Instruction (Mertes, 2013, dissertation)
notes: Abstract only. A single rural middle school pilot comparing ALEKS with direct instruction in grades 6 to 8; the abstract states no eligibility rule and does not say which students or classes were in each arm, so unclear rather than universal. Kraft n 2500 is implausible for one rural middle school and could not be checked; flag. The design reads as a comparison of instruction methods rather than a randomised trial.

evidence_quote: RAND Europe found in a UK randomised controlled trial that classes of 8 and 9 year-old primary school children randomly allocated to receive a technology-based education intervention using Microsoft's Immersive Reader performed as well as business-as-usual classes.
resolved_title: Evaluation of a Technology-based Intervention for Reading in UK Classroom Settings (Sutherland et al., 2019, RAND Europe RR-4208)
notes: Abstract only (69 words). Whole classes of 8 and 9 year olds (UK Years 4 and 5) randomised; no student rule stated, but the abstract is thin, so a reviewer could prefer unclear. Kraft n 635-2133 with two effects could not be checked; the smaller n may be an FSM subgroup. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Sutherland, Conroy et al. 2018, early childhood) and was ignored.

evidence_quote: the effects of collaborative strategic reading and metacognitive strategic learning on the reading comprehension of students in seventh- and eighth-grade English/language arts classes in two sites (Texas, Colorado) and in three school districts. Students were randomly assigned to classes and then classes were randomly assigned to treatment or business-as-usual comparison groups.
resolved_title: Efficacy of Collaborative Strategic Reading With Middle School Students (Vaughn et al., 2011, American Educational Research Journal)
notes: Abstract only. Intact grade 7 and 8 English/language arts classes in three districts, 61 classes randomised; no achievement or demographic rule stated. Kraft n 782 could not be checked against the abstract. Confidence capped at medium by the abstract-only rule.
